parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French azimut, from Arabic اَلسَّمْت (as-samt, “direction”). See cenit.
From Old French adober (“to knight, equip”), from Germanic.
From Old French [Term?], from Latin alligāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Old French alier, from Latin alligāre (“to bind”). Cognate with English ally.
From Old French healmet, ultimately from Germanic origin.

From the Old French ancestrel, from the noun ancestre (“ancestor”), from Late Latin antecessor (“predecessor”), an agent noun from the past participle stem of Latin antecedere (“to proceed”), from the prefix ante- with the infinitive cedere (“to go”), the latter from Proto-Italic *kezdō (“to avoid o
From Old French ancestre (compare Modern French ancêtre), from Latin antecessor. Doublet of antecesor.
From Old French antelop, from Medieval Latin antilops, from Byzantine Greek ἀνθόλοψ (anthólops).
Inherited from Old Spanish arcipreste, arçipreste (early 13th c.), borrowed from Old French arciprestre, arcepreste (whence modern French archiprêtre), from Medieval Latin archipresbyter.
Borrowed from Old French harnais.
Borrowed from Old French harpeau, from harper (“to grab”), from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ (“harp”).
Borrowed from Old French bandon.
Borrowed from Old French bank, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz. Compare English bench and bank.
From Old French ban (“public declaration”) or bandon, influenced by the word above.

Inherited from Old Spanish barato (“low price”), from baratar (“to cheat (in sales)”), from Old French barateor (“swindler, deceiver”), from barate (“strife, fraud”); see barater. Compare French baratter and Irish brath (“treachery”), and also English barter.
From Old Spanish baron, from Old French baron. Doublet of varón.
From Old French baston (“stick, truncheon”); related to modern French bâton, Italian bastone. Cognate with English baton.

parole.significato: rowboat for four rowers and a cox
parole.testo: From Old French batel (“boat”).
From Old French bossel, diminutive of boce (“knob-like swelling”).

Borrowed from Old French vogue, from the verb voguer (“to sway, move along”), from Old Italian vogare, of Germanic origin, from Old Saxon wagon (“to float, move as in waves”). Related to modern French vogue (“wave; course of success”), and the verb voguer (“move through the water”). Compare Italian
Via Old French bouter (“to strike”) (modern French bouter), from Frankish *buttan, from Frankish *bautan (“to hit, strike”). Compare French bouter, Portuguese botar and Italian buttare.
From Old French boton (Modern French bouton). Cognate with English button, Italian bottone, Portuguese botão.
Inherited from Old Spanish broquer, broquell (1368), from Old French boucler, bocler, bucler (French bouclier), from Vulgar Latin *bucculārius (“bossed”), from Latin buccula (“boss”).
Most likely from Old French bouffante, present participle of bouffer (“to puff up”) (compare imitative origins of both Medieval Latin buffa and English puff).

Inherited from Old Spanish chanciller, from Old French chancelier, from Late Latin cancellārius. The modern form probably results from the influence of the learned form cancelario, borrowed from the Latin directly.
Inherited from Old Spanish canela, borrowed from Old French canele, borrowed from Italian cannella, from canna (“pipe”) + -ella.

From Old Spanish carcax, from Old French carcois, carquais, tarquait, tarchais, borrowed in turn from Byzantine Greek καρκάσιον (karkásion), a medieval variant of ταρκάσιον (tarkásion), from Arabic تِرْكَاش (tirkāš), from Persian تیرکش (tirkaš). The -x in Old Spanish may be due to Old Catalan carcax

Borrowed from Old French chamberlayn, chamberlenc (“chamberlain”), from Frankish *kamarling (“chamberlain”), equivalent to *kamer (“chamber”) + *-ling (“-ling”). Cognate with Old High German chamarling (“chamberlain”). Doublet of camarlengo

parole.significato: dignitary in charge of the royal seal
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, borrowed from Old French chancelier, from Late Latin cancellarius.
Borrowed from Old French chalemie.
From Old Spanish chimenea, from older cheminea (via vowel metathesis), from Old French cheminee, from Late Latin camīnāta. Compare English chimney.
Borrowed from Old French chalemie, from Late Latin calamellus (“little reed”). Compare French chalumeau and Middle English shalemye. Doublet of caramelo and caramillo.
Possibly from Old French cholle (“head”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *keula (“mace”), earlier "lump, lump of coal," from Proto-Germanic *kulą.
Borrowed from Old French sicamor, from Latin sycomorus, from Ancient Greek συκόμορος (sukómoros).

Likely from Old French cisel, from cisoir (with a change in suffix), from Late Latin cīsōrium (“cutting instrument”), ultimately from Latin caedere (“cut”). The /n/ seems to have been taken from pincel (“paintbrush”).

parole.significato: swan (any of various species of large, long-necked waterfowl, of genus Cygnus)
parole.testo: From Old French cisne, from Late Latin cicinus, from Latin cycnus, ultimately from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos, “swan”).
Borrowed from Old French colche (“bed, couch”) (cf. modern French couche), ultimately from Latin collocō (“put in place”).
Borrowed from Old French conestable, influenced by conde (“count”), from Late Latin comes stabulī (“officer of the stables”).
Inherited from Old Spanish coral, from Old French coral, from Latin corallium, from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion).
Borrowed from Old French corsier. The alteration of the second r to l is an instance of phonetic dissimilation.
Borrowed from Old French cospel.
From Old French cote, from Latin cotta (“undercoat, tunic”), see also German Kotze and Kutte.
Borrowed from Old French dameisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella. Doublet of doncella.
Inherited from Old Spanish dardo (c. 1250), from Old French dart, from Frankish *darōþu.
Borrowed from Old French desmanteler. By surface analysis, des- + mantel + -ar.

parole.significato: to cause a person to faint
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French esmaier (“to perturb”), from Latin *magāre, from Frankish *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą. Cognate with English dismay although a false friend. Compare Portuguese desmaiar. Doublet and related to esmayao "to be hungry, famished", from esmayar.
Borrowed from Old French deien, from Late Latin decānus, from Latin decem (“ten”). Doublet of decano, a borrowing from Latin, and of the rare or archaic degano, an inherited term.

From Old French diamant, from Latin adamantem (“hardest steel; diamond”), influenced by δια- (dia-); from Ancient Greek ἀδάμᾱς (adámās, “unconquerable, invincible”). Doublet of imán. More at English diamond.
Inherited from Old Spanish debuxar, from Old French deboissier.
Borrowed from Old French douelle, diminutive of doue, from Latin doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ). Compare Portuguese aduela, Galician doela. Doublet of doga.
From Old French douçaine, doucine.
Borrowed from Old French duc, from Latin dux. Doublet of dogo and dux.
Borrowed from Old French empeechier, from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”).

parole.significato: to hire, to employ (to give someone a job)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French empleiier, variant of emploiier (compare modern French employer), from Latin implicāre. Doublet of implicar, borrowed directly from Latin. Cf. also the Old Spanish form emplegar, which may have been inherited; compare the surviving Asturian emplegar.
From Old Spanish engendrar, probably borrowed from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre.
Borrowed from Old French ensembler.

Borrowed from Old French *escoinz (“nook”), nominative case of Old French escoinçon, escoinson (whence modern French écoinçon), from Old French coin, coing (“nook, corner”), from Latin cuneus (“wedge”).
From Old French score, from Dutch schoor.
From Old French escote, from Frankish *skōta.
Deverbal from escotar, from cota, or borrowed from Old French escot, from Frankish.
Borrowed from Old French escoutillon.

Borrowed from Old French esmaier (“to perturb”). Doublet of desmayar. Cognate with Galician esmayar. desmayar and esmayar used to be interchangeable, but esmayar is now obsolete and only found in its adjective form esmayado or more commonly esmayao (being hungry or famished), in southern Spanish dia

From Old Spanish esmeralda, possibly through the intermediate of Old French esmeralde (Modern French émeraude), from Vulgar Latin *smeralda, *smaraldus, alteration of Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), of Semitic origin. Cf. also the Old Spanish form esmaragde.

Inherited from Old Spanish esmerejón, esmerijón, calque of Old French esmerillon, diminutive of esmeril, from Medieval Latin smerillus, from Proto-West Germanic *smiril, from Proto-Germanic *smirilaz.
From Old French estache (“stake”)
Borrowed from Old French estandart. Doublet of estándar, via English.
From Old French estay, from Frankish *staka (“stake, post”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô.
From Old French stofe (“stuff, material”).
From Old French estoc (“end of a sword”).
From Old French estribord, a Germanic loanword (see also German steuerbord, German Low German stürbord, Old Norse stjornborði). Equivalent to English steer + board.
Relatinized from Old French estrangier. Adjectival cognate with English strange and French étrange (“strange, foreign”). Nominal cognate with English stranger and French étranger.

parole.significato: a sharp point left where cloth has been cut away on the edge of a flag, curtain, etc.; fringe, tail
parole.testo: From obsolete farpar (“scratch, claw, rend”), a borrowing of Old French harper (“grasp forcefully”) from Proto-Germanic *hrapōną (“scrape”). Related to Spanish harapo (“rag”).
Borrowed from Old French felon.
From Old French ferret (“branding iron”), diminutive of fer (“iron”), from Latin ferrum.
Inherited from Old Spanish flecha, frecha, borrowed from Old French fleche, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia, of Frankish origin.

parole.significato: florin (any unit of currency called thus)
parole.testo: From Old French florin, from Italian fiorino. Doublet of forinto.
Borrowed from Old French frise.
Borrowed from Old French gabinet, diminutive of cabane, from Occitan cabana.
From Old French gale (“rejoicing”), from galer (“to enjoy oneself”). Ultimately cognate to gallant and hence probably from Frankish *wala (“good, well”).
Borrowed from Old French galoper.
From Old French garant, probably from Frankish *werênd, *warjan, akin to German gewähren (“to grant”) and Old High German wërênt.
From Old French garite (“watchtower”) (modern French guérite), from guarir (“to protect”).
From Old French canivet, from late Old English cnīf (“knife”) + -et, from Old Norse knívr, from Proto-Germanic *knībaz.
From Old French girfaut, gerfault or Provençal gerfalt, gerfalc, both from Old Norse geirfalki, from geiri (“a type of dart”) + falki (“hawk”) (because of the resemblance to the bird's plumage).
From Old French gigue.

From Old French gons, gonz, gont (whence modern French gond), from Latin gomphus, from Ancient Greek γόμφος (gómphos), from Proto-Hellenic *gómpʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos. First attested in early 15th century.

Metathesis of gonce, from Old French gons, gonz, gont (whence modern French gond), from Latin gomphus, from Ancient Greek γόμφος (gómphos), from Proto-Hellenic *gómpʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos. First attested in early 15th century.

Inherited from Old Spanish granja (“barn”), from Old French grange, Vulgar Latin *grānica (“grain storage barn, granary; grange, small farm”), from Latin grānum (“grain”) from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Cognate with English grange and Italian grangia.

From Old French graal, grael, from Medieval Latin gradālis (“cup”), of unclear origin. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *crātālis, from *crātus, from Ancient Greek κρᾱτήρ (krātḗr, “mixing bowl, wassail bowl”).

Metathetic form of guirlanda, from Old French garlande, garlaunde, gerlande, guerlande (compare French guirlande), from Frankish *wierlōn, *wieralōn, a frequentative form of Frankish *wierōn (“to adorn, bedeck”), from *wiera (“a gold thread”), akin to Old High German wieren (“to adorn”), wiara (“gol
From Old French gargoule (“spout”).

parole.significato: axe, hatchet (tool for felling trees or chopping wood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish facha, borrowed from Old French hache, of Germanic origin.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter H/h.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French ache, from Vulgar Latin *acca.
From halcón (“hawk”) + gerifalte (“gyrfalcon”), from Old French girfalt, gerfalt.
Derived from Old Spanish harpar (“to shred, tear”), from Old French harper; perhaps influenced by trapo (“cloth”).

Inherited from Old Spanish ervage, erbaje, erbage, herbaje, herbage (c. 1250), from Old French erbage, from Early Medieval Latin herbāticum, from Latin herba (“grass”). By surface analysis, hierba + -aje. Doublet of herbazgo.
Inherited from Old Spanish hopa (c. 1378), of uncertain further origin. Probably from some dialectal clipping of Old French houppelande.

Inherited from Old Spanish aymant, apocopic form of aymante (“lodestone”), from Old French aïmant (“lodestone”), from Vulgar Latin *adimas, from Latin adamās (“very hard steel; adamant; diamond”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas), with the same meaning. Reinforced or reintroduced by mod
Borrowed from Old French angleis, from Old English Englisc. Compare Portuguese inglês and Italian inglese.
Inherited from Old Spanish haca, from Old French haque, from Middle English hack, from the Middle English equivalent of Hackney, a borough of London famous for its horses.
Inherited from Old Spanish jargonça, from Old French jagonce.

Inherited from Old Spanish ja(v)ola, borrowed from Old French jaiole, from Late Latin caveola, from Latin cavea (“cage”) + -ola (diminutive ending). Doublet of gayola, which was inherited. Cognates include English jail.

parole.significato: chief; president; head; leader of a business, political party, or other organization
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish xefe, from Old French chief, from Latin caput. Compare Portuguese chefe. Doublet of cabo and chef.
Borrowed from Old French joie, alternative form of jouel (source of modern French joyau and Spanish joyel), from Latin jocus.
From Old French joiel.

parole.significato: language (the ability to communicate using words)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish lenguage, borrowed from Old French language or Old Occitan lenguatge, both from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, derived from Latin lingua. By surface analysis, lengua + -aje. Cognate with English language.

From Latin ligāre, possibly through the intermediate of Old French lier in the Middle Ages, as it appeared relatively late in Spanish texts. See also the doublet ligar, a semi-learned term, as well as the inherited Old Spanish form legar (“to tie, bind”) (in modern Spanish, this word survives as a r
Inherited from Old Spanish ligero, borrowed from Old French legier (modern French léger), from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin levis.
Inherited from Old Spanish malla, borrowed from Old French maille (modern maille), from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula. Doublet of mácula and mancha.
Borrowed from Old French mareschal, from Early Medieval Latin mariscalcus, from Frankish *marhaskalk (“equerry”), from *marh (“horse”) + *skalk (“servant”), from Proto-Germanic *marhaz + *skalkaz.

Borrowed from Old French markis, marchis; from Late Latin marchēnsis, from Old High German marcha, from Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”).
From Old French mast (modern mât).
From Old French mastin (modern French mâtin (“guard dog”)), from Vulgar Latin *mansuetīnus (“tamed (animal)”), from Latin mānsuetus (“tamed”).
Inherited from Old Spanish maçonero, from Old French maçon.
Inherited from Old Spanish montar, borrowed from Old French monter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre, from Latin montem.

parole.significato: mast (a tall, slim post or tower used to support the sails on a ship)
parole.testo: From mástel, from maste, from Old French mast (modern mât), with influence from árbol.
From Old French oripel.
Borrowed from Old French pacque, borrowed from Middle Dutch pak, from Old Dutch *pakko, from Frankish *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkō.

parole.significato: a round shallow tray, pan, or bowl
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French paele, from Latin patella. Doublet of padilla, paella, and puela.
Borrowed from Old French païsan, itself from Latin pagus (“countryside”).
Borrowed from Old French panel.
From parche + -ar, from Old French parche (“leather, sheepskin”), from Latin Parthĭca (pellis) (literally “leather of Parthia”).
Borrowed from Old French parche, from Latin parthica (pellis) (“Parthian (leather)”).
From Old French pastel. Cognate with English pastel.
Via Old French and Occitan from Latin pila.
From Old French pennon, diminutive of penne (“feather”), from Latin penna (“feather, wing”).
Borrowed from Old French portage, from Late Latin portāticum. Doublet of portazgo, which was inherited.
Inherited from Old Spanish preste, prestre, borrowed from Old French prestre, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Doublet of presbítero.
From Old French ralée (“going, rush of a hunting bird on its prey”).
From Old French realme, reialme, reaume (“kingdom”). Compare to English realm.

parole.significato: to reject, to turn down, to turn away, to refuse, to dismiss, to shun, to decline
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French rechacier, from chacier (modern chasser), from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, whence also Spanish cazar. Compare Portuguese rechaçar.
Inherited from Old Spanish renta, from Old French rente, from Medieval Latin rendita.

parole.significato: a type of roundelay from Spain
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French randon. Doublet of rándom, borrowed from English.
Borrowed from Old French rostir, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *hraustjan, *rōstjan (“to roast”), from Proto-West Germanic *raustijan, see also Old High German rôsten (modern German rösten).

parole.significato: rhubarb (any plant of the genus Rheum)
parole.testo: From Old French reubarbe, from Late Latin reubarbarum, probably from Koine Greek ῥῆον βαρβαρικόν (rhêon barbarikón).
Borrowed from Old French jarser. Compare Galician sarxar and French gercer.
From Old French jansier.
Borrowed from Old French sidre, from Latin sīcera, from Ancient Greek σῑ́κερᾰ (sī́keră), from Hebrew שכר.
Borrowed from Old French sirop. Doublet of jarabe.

Related to the verb soslayar (“to place obliquely”), from Old Spanish deslayer (“to go outside the tangent”), from Old French d'eslais (“impetuously”), from s'esslaisier (“to throw with impetus”), from laissier (“to leave”).
Probably borrowed from Old French til, from Latin tilia, with a shift in gender.
From Old French toer, from Old Norse toga (“to pull something”).

Apparently from Old French tialz (“area between the stern and mainmast, awning”), borrowed from Old Norse tjald or another Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *teldą. See also Middle Dutch telt, Old High German zelt and Old Norse tjald. Cognate with English tilt (“tent fabric and covering”).

Inherited from Old Spanish tonel, borrowed from Old French tonel (“barrel”), diminutive of tone (“large barrel”), from Late Latin tunna. Probably entered through Old Galician-Portuguese or Old Aragonese, where it seems to have been borrowed earlier. Cognate with Galician and Portuguese tonel and Cat

parole.significato: metric ton (a unit of mass equal to exactly 1000 kg)
parole.testo: From tonel (“tun”) + -ada (“-ful”), from Old French tonel (“little tun, cask”), from tone + -el (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from Late Latin tunna (“tun”), from Proto-Celtic *tunna (“hide, skin”). In reference to the English unit, calqued from English ton. Cognate with Galician and Portuguese ton
From Old French top (“top, summit”), from Frankish *top; compare English top.
Probably a blend of Old French tresce (“tress”) and trena (“sash”) (Vulgar Latin *trena << Latin trina (“triple”)). Possibly influenced by tres (“three”). Compare French tresse, Italian treccia.
Borrowed from Old French trenchier.

According to Coromines and Pascual, from Old Spanish trufán, attested since the 13th century, borrowed from Old French truand (“a mendicant; a crook or gangster”), from a Gaulish *trūgantos, perhaps diminutive of *trūgos, cognate with English truant, Irish trogán, related to Old Irish tróg (“miserab
From Old French oltrage, from Latin ultra (“beyond”). Cognate with English outrage.
Probably from Old French vire (“dart, welt”), from Vulgar Latin *veria (“javelin, dart”), from Latin verua.
Borrowed from Old French eschirgaite or eschargaite, from Frankish *skarawahta, from *skara (“troop”) (from Proto-Germanic *skarō (“portion, share”)) + *wahta (“watch, guard”).
